Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

knowledge noun

awareness: without my knowledge, to my knowledge

also without my knowledge, to my knowledge, to the best of my knowledge, knowingly, unknowingly, behind my back

classical

Cic. Fam. 5.2.3: nihil … mē īnsciente esse factum
Plaut. Trin. 167: mē apsente atque īnsciente

mē īnsciente

ablative absolute with īnsciēns, īnscientis, not knowing; likewise tē, eō īnsciente

without my knowledge

Other words

  • clam (+ accusative) — without the knowledge of, behind someone’s back

    also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 98: haec clam mē omnia; Caes. BC 2.32.8, with the ablative: clam vōbīs; Traupman 337

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra)

    As a preposition, the Latin of comedy; classical prose uses clam as an adverb, “secretly” (Lewis & Short).

  • quod sciam — to my knowledge, as far as I know

    relative clause with the subjunctive · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.59: nūllae, quod sciam; Plaut., Ter. (Lewis & Short)

    See know.

  • sciēns, scientis — knowingly, with full knowledge, on purpose

    present participle of sciō, used as an adjective · also used · classical · Cic. Ac. 2.146: sī sciēns falleret; Plaut. Poen. 112: dissimulat sciēns sē scīre · Declension on Wiktionary

Examples

  • tantum tē suspicārī volō, nihil in eā rē per conlēgam meum mē īnsciente esse factum

    I only want you to suspect that nothing in that business was done by my colleague without my knowledgeCic. Fam. 5.2.3

  • mē apsente atque īnsciente, incōnsultū meō

    while I was away, without my knowledge, without asking mePlaut. Trin. 167

  • et is omnīs linguās scit, sed dissimulat sciēns sē scīre

    and he knows every language, but knowingly pretends that he does notPlaut. Poen. 112

See also know, knowledge.

SourcesLewis & Short: insciens · Lewis & Short: clam · Lewis & Short: scio

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 337, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).

Cicero (Fam. 5.2.3, Ac. 2.146), Plautus (Trin. 167, Poen. 112), Terence (Heaut. 98) and Caesar (BC 2.32.8) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).

Plautus and Terence are quoted in the spelling of the Perseus texts (apsente, omnīs).

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
